title: The Paper Ledger
premise: In the winter of 1917, Casper Ravensworth, a battlefield nurse whose ledger records the names of dead soldiers that officers omit from official reports, is stranded when the only bridge out of the valley closes for the season. Trapped at a decaying field hospital with a found family of orderlies, deserters, and wounded men, Casper must smuggle the ledger past three military checkpoints before spring floods destroy the evidence and the officers responsible are quietly promoted. The journey costs them allies, safety, and finally their anonymity — but by delivering the names to a war correspondent, Casper ensures the forgotten are remembered, even as they must surrender their own name to survive.
about_author: Tamsin Vane is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing unsent letters from the First World War. They write historical fiction about the people history files under 'miscellaneous.'

chapters.title: What the Officers Omit
chapters.summary: Casper's POV. At the Valmont field hospital, Casper records in a hidden ledger the names of eleven men left off the official death rolls after a failed advance. The emotional beat is quiet defiance: memory as an act of resistance no one has ordered.

chapters.title: The Bridge Closes
chapters.summary: Casper's POV. Word arrives that the Pont-Aubert bridge is closed for the season; supply convoys stop, and Major Halloway orders all personal papers inventoried. Casper hides the ledger inside a hymnal. The beat is dread — the trap closing without a sound.

chapters.title: The Family We Improvise
chapters.summary: Ensemble chapter anchored in orderly Bram Tull's POV. Introduces the hospital's makeshift family: Bram, cook Odile, shell-shocked private Wren, and Dr. Ilsa Marchetti. They share contraband coffee and stories. The beat is warmth discovered in scarcity — found family forming.

chapters.title: Halloway's Arithmetic
chapters.summary: Casper's POV. Major Halloway audits casualty figures to protect Colonel Verrek's reputation, and Casper realizes the omissions aren't clerical error but deliberate erasure tied to a court-martial cover-up. The beat is cold clarity: this is not negligence, it is policy.

chapters.title: Wren Remembers Nothing
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. The shell-shocked private fragments recall the same advance that produced the omitted names — he may be a living witness. Casper gently interviews him. The beat is fragile hope entangled with guilt over using a broken man's memory.

chapters.title: Three Checkpoints, One Winter
chapters.summary: Casper and Bram's shared POV, alternating scenes. They map the route: the mill checkpoint, the garrison at Saint-Lys, and the bridgehead itself. Each demands papers they cannot forge convincingly. The beat is sober planning — courage measured in logistics.

chapters.title: Odile's Kitchen Table
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. The cook reveals she once smuggled letters for the Resistance-adjacent network in 1915 and offers her bread cart as transport. The family debates the cost: if caught, everyone loses everything. The beat is commitment — choosing each other over safety.

chapters.title: The Inventory
chapters.summary: Casper's POV. Halloway's surprise inspection nearly finds the hymnal; Dr. Marchetti covers with a forged diagnosis, burning her own credibility with the command. The beat is terror and gratitude — the first debt of the conspiracy is paid in someone else's skin.

chapters.title: Names in the Snow
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. A soldier dies of wounds before his name can be confirmed; Casper reads the ledger aloud over his grave, adding him properly. Wren begins to stabilize, anchoring himself to the ritual. The beat is grief transmuted into purpose.

chapters.title: The Mill at Dusk
chapters.summary: Bram's POV. First checkpoint run: Bram carries the ledger in flour sacks through the mill checkpoint, bluffing a sergeant who knew his brother. He passes — but the sergeant now remembers his face. The beat is relief shadowed by new vulnerability.

chapters.title: Verrek Comes Down the Mountain
chapters.summary: Casper's POV. Colonel Verrek visits to bury the record personally, promoting Halloway and ordering the hospital's records burned for 'hygiene.' Casper saves two pages by memorizing them overnight. The beat is fury held behind a nurse's calm face.

chapters.title: What Ilsa Owes
chapters.summary: Dr. Marchetti's POV. Flashback to her disgraced testimony years ago; she recognizes Verrek's method because it destroyed her career. She gives Casper the garrison pass codes. The beat is redemption offered late but accepted anyway.

chapters.title: Betrayal at the Bread Cart
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. An informant — lonely clerk Petit — tips off the garrison; Odile is detained and the cart searched. She swallows nothing, confesses nothing, but the ledger was not aboard. The beat is sacrifice and the narrowing of time.

chapters.title: Petit's Conscience
chapters.summary: Petit's POV. The clerk, sick with guilt, warns Casper that Wren's medical file has been flagged and Wren will be transferred — and interrogated — within days. The beat is moral awakening in a small man who thought himself invisible too.

chapters.title: Everything That Can Be Carried
chapters.summary: Casper's POV. The title beat: Casper packs the ledger, Wren's file, Marchetti's codes, and almost nothing else, measuring their whole life into one satchel. Farewells at the kitchen table. The beat is tender renunciation — leaving the family to save the names.

chapters.title: Saint-Lys Garrison
chapters.summary: Dual POV, Casper and Wren. Second checkpoint: Casper poses as a transfer escort using Marchetti's codes while Wren, half-lucid, accidentally corroborates the story with a fragment of true memory. The beat is improvised trust paying off against impossible odds.

chapters.title: The Frozen River
chapters.summary: Bram's POV. With the bridgehead alerted, Bram guides them onto the frozen river below the bridge — the route no one guards because no one survives it. Ice cracks; supplies are abandoned. The beat is terror stripped to essentials: carry the names or die meaninglessly.

chapters.title: Checkpoint Three
chapters.summary: Casper's POV. Climax begins: at the bridgehead, Halloway himself waits, having deduced everything. He offers Casper amnesty for the ledger and silence about the family. The beat is temptation — survival offered at the price of every name in the book.

chapters.title: The Reading
chapters.summary: Climax, ensemble POV. Casper refuses and instead reads the ledger aloud to the assembled soldiers on the bridge, name after name, until the ranks themselves become witnesses Halloway cannot arrest. Wren stands and recites the final page from memory. The beat is triumphant exposure.

chapters.title: After the Ice Breaks
chapters.summary: Bram's POV. Spring floods take the bridge; in the chaos, the ledger reaches war correspondent Elias Brandt waiting on the far bank. Halloway, undone by public witnesses, lets them go rather than create martyrs. The beat is exhausted, hard-won escape.

chapters.title: The Names in Print
chapters.summary: Casper's POV. Weeks later, Brandt's article runs with all forty-one names; inquiries begin, Verrek is quietly relieved of command. Casper learns Odile, Marchetti, and Petit survived detention. The beat is bittersweet justice — partial, slow, but real.

chapters.title: A New Ledger
chapters.summary: Casper's POV, epilogue. The found family reunites at Odile's rebuilt kitchen; Casper opens a fresh notebook and writes the first new entry — not the dead, but the living, beginning with their own true name. The beat is homecoming: memory kept, identity reclaimed.
